label: Place
name: Nigeria
summary:
Nigeria, officially the Federal Republic of Nigeria, is a country in West Africa between the Sahel to the north and the Gulf of Guinea to the south. With approximately 220 million people, it is the most populous country in Africa and the sixth-most populous in the world. Nigeria's oil reserves — among the largest in Africa — make it the continent's largest oil producer and the largest economy by GDP, though deep poverty, inequality, and corruption have constrained its development potential.

The territory of modern Nigeria has hosted advanced civilizations for over 2,000 years. The Nok culture (500 BCE–200 CE) produced West Africa's earliest known terracotta sculptures. The Kanem-Bornu Empire dominated the Lake Chad basin for over 1,000 years (700–1900 CE). The Yoruba city-states, Igbo societies, and the Sokoto Caliphate (1804–1903) — the largest state in Africa at its peak — all flourished in the region before British colonization. The Royal Niger Company's commercial penetration (1880s) and the formal British colonial acquisition (1914) merged northern and southern Nigeria into a single administrative unit that had no historical precedent.

Independence in 1960 was followed by the catastrophic Biafra War (1967–1970), which killed 1–3 million people, mostly through famine. Military rule dominated from 1966 to 1999, punctuated by brief civilian governments. Democratic consolidation since 1999 has been achieved despite chronic insecurity (Boko Haram in the northeast, banditry in the northwest), but Nigeria's demographic weight — expected to surpass the US in population by 2050 — makes its political trajectory one of the most consequential in the world.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nigeria's ancient civilizations, such as the Nok culture and Kanem-Bornu Empire, laid foundational knowledge for modern West African societies. The country's strategic location has facilitated trade and cultural exchange across the continent.

causes: Diverse pre-colonial civilizations (Nok, Kanem-Bornu, Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa-Fulani states) creating the heterogeneous cultural base of modern Nigeria
British colonial amalgamation of 1914 merging Northern and Southern Nigeria into an artificial single unit that had no historical precedent
Oil discovery (1956) and the post-independence oil boom transforming Nigeria's economy and politics around petroleum rents
Biafra War (1967–1970) cementing federalism and military dominance as the defining features of post-independence governance
effects: Most populous country in Africa (220 million) — projected to be the world's third-most populous country by 2050
Biafra War (1967–1970) killing 1–3 million and becoming the paradigmatic post-colonial African civil war
Nigerian literary tradition — Chinua Achebe, Wole Soyinka (Nobel 1986), Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie — among the most celebrated in world literature
Nollywood film industry — world's second-largest film producer by volume — a major force in African cultural soft power
